newsitem.title: CROATIA: EU official warns Croatia on democracy.
newsitem.headline: EU official warns Croatia on democracy.

text.p: Croatia must improve its flawed democracy or risk losing the seat in the Council of Europe won last week, a European Union official said in a Croatian newspaper interview published on Thursday.
The Council kept Croatia at arm's length for years in protest at human rights abuses and doubts about its commitment to peace in former Yugoslavia, notably Bosnia.

But the Council, antechamber to the EU, finally decided to accept Croatia to reward it for forming diplomatic ties with old war enemy Serbia, enacting a war amnesty for its own Serb minority and bolstering Bosnia's peace process.

The EU official said that while Croatia's democracy remained flawed, it could not have been indefinitely ostracised by the Council because countries with similar problems like Russia and Albania were already members.

But this did not mean Croatia could rest on its laurels if it wanted to stay in the Council and progress towards EU integration, Rene van der Linden, chairman of the 40-nation Council's political committee, was quoted as saying.
"The problems which led to postponement of Croatia's admission have unfortunately not been solved," he was quoted by the independent weekly Nacional as saying.

"Croatia, like Albania and Russia, still has to fulfil many obligations ... on human rights and rights of national minorities ... The Croatian government will be given a deadline by which it has to fulfil these obligations.

"If Croatia fails to meet (them)... the Council assembly will have to take the drastic step of withdrawing credentials of Croatian deputies, by which Croatia would be excluded from the work of the Council, and from the body itself."

He said Croatia must boost its democratic performance in three key ways -- allow Serb war refugees who fled abroad to resettle in former homes, stop hounding and repressing independent media and accept opposition victories in elections.
On paper, Croatia is a multi-party democracy that guarantees minority rights and freedom of expression.
But human-rights activists say minority Serbs continue to be treated as second-class citizens vulnerable to assault and eviction by Croats without proper legal recourse.
President Franjo Tudjman has refused to recognise an opposition coalition victory over his HDZ party in elections for the patronage-rich Zagreb regional government a year ago.
Citing "national security" concerns, he has appointed an indefinite HDZ caretaker administration.

"Regarding the Zagreb crisis, the Croatian government must know it cannot put off resolving it forever. This problem is not just about naming a new mayor but recognising the result of elections," van der Linden was quoted as saying.
"New elections will have to be held."
Van der Linden said the Council would form a special monitoring mission in Croatia by January to check on the extent of Croatian compliance with membership obligations.
